Frequently Asked Questions

Common Questions, Straight Answers

No spin, no campaign language. Just the facts you need to make an informed vote on June 18.

Voting & Polling Places

Election Day

June 18, 2026

Polls open 7:00 am – close at 8:00 pm

All registered voters in Evergreen vote on Measure L. You do not need to own property — any registered voter can participate.

Find your polling placeVote.gov or call the Evergreen County Elections Office: (555) 234-5678
Registration deadline has passedIf you're already registered, you're ready. First-time voter? Conditional ballots may be available at the polls — call (555) 234-5678.
What to bringA photo ID is helpful but may not be required in all cases. Your sample ballot will list Measure L.

Your polling place is assigned based on your registered address. To find it: visit vote.gov, enter your address, and look for "June 18, 2026 Evergreen Local Election." You can also call the Evergreen County Elections Office at (555) 234-5678 (Mon–Fri, 8am–5pm) or email elections@evergreencounty.gov. Polls are open 7:00 am to 8:00 pm on June 18.

Yes. If you're a registered voter in Evergreen but didn't receive a vote-by-mail ballot (or you lost it), you can vote in person at your assigned polling place on June 18. You may be asked to cast a provisional ballot, which will be counted once your registration is verified. Bring any ID you have to speed up the process.

Cost & Funding

For the average Evergreen household, Measure L costs approximately $3.20 per month, or about $38 per year. The exact amount varies based on the assessed value of your property. Renters: the measure is assessed against property owners, not tenants, although as with all property taxes it may eventually be reflected in rents.

  • Average household: ~$3.20/month
  • Median-value home: ~$3.85/month
  • Small commercial property: varies by value

Measure L establishes a special assessment with a 10-year initial term. At the end of 10 years, voters will have the opportunity to renew it. The measure includes annual public audits and a citizen oversight committee to ensure funds are spent as described. All spending is reported publicly each year.

No. Measure L funds are dedicated solely to library operations by the language of the measure itself. The city council cannot redirect the funds to other uses. Covered expenses include staff salaries, building maintenance, programming, collection materials, and technology. A citizen oversight committee reviews spending annually, and a public audit is filed with the city each year.

Private Donations vs. Public Funding

No. Private donations cannot replace public funding. Here's why, plainly:

  • The Friends of the Library and individual donors provide wonderful supplemental funding for special programs, new collections, and special events. But they cannot sustain daily operations.
  • The library's operating budget covers 12 full-time staff positions, utilities, insurance, building maintenance, and daily operations — costs that run to hundreds of thousands of dollars per year.
  • Private donations in a community of our size are unpredictable year to year. A library cannot hire or retain staff based on fundraising projections.
  • Public libraries are a public good — like roads, parks, and fire protection. They require stable public funding, not the charitable economy.

That said, if you'd like to give to the library directly, contact the Friends of the Library at friends@evergreenlib.org. Campaign donations go to voter outreach, not the library itself.

The city council has reviewed the general fund and concluded that there is no available surplus to maintain current library funding levels without cutting other essential services. The library currently receives general fund appropriations, but these are subject to annual budget battles and can be cut without voter approval. Measure L creates dedicated, protected funding that cannot be raided for other purposes. It also removes the library from the annual appropriations process, giving it the stability to plan long-term and retain experienced staff.

If Measure L Fails

The library director has announced that beginning July 1, 2026, the following cuts will be implemented if Measure L does not pass:

  • 18 weekly open hours cut — approximately 3 hours per day
  • Sunday closures — the library will no longer open on Sundays
  • After-school homework help program eliminated
  • Summer youth reading program reduced by 40%
  • Story time sessions reduced from 5 to 2 per week
  • Building repairs suspended, including the leaking roof in the children's wing
  • Hiring freeze with possible layoffs if budget shortfalls continue
  • Computer lab hours reduced

These are not hypothetical. The library has already begun internal planning for these reductions pending the election outcome.

Technically yes, but in practice it is very difficult. Once programs are eliminated, staff leave, institutional knowledge is lost, and community trust erodes. Library funding measures typically need to return to voters, and experience in other cities shows that re-building services after cuts takes years and costs significantly more than maintaining them in the first place. Voting yes on June 18 is far easier and cheaper than rebuilding later.

Politics & Partisanship

No. Measure L is a non-partisan local funding measure. Library supporters include Democrats, Republicans, independents, and people who rarely vote in any election. Our endorsers include faith leaders, business owners, teachers, parents, and retirees from across the political spectrum. The library serves everyone regardless of politics, and this measure has been intentionally kept free of partisan endorsements. We have no position on any candidate, party, or other ballot measure. We just want to keep the library open.

As of the publication date of this website, we are not aware of an organized, funded opposition campaign against Measure L. There is no opposition committee registered with the city. Some residents have expressed concerns about cost or the use of public funds, which we address directly in our FAQ. If you've seen opposition materials, we'd encourage you to look at who filed them and what their specific concerns are — and to weigh those against the concrete, announced service cuts that will happen if the measure fails.

How to Help

Here are the highest-impact things you can do right now, in order of impact:

  1. Vote yourself on June 18 — obvious but essential. Find your polling place at vote.gov.
  2. Tell three people — personal conversations with friends, neighbors, and family are the single most effective form of political persuasion. Text three people you know in Evergreen and ask them to vote yes.
  3. Volunteer tonight or on Election Day — sign up for a shift. Phone banking tonight, poll greeter shifts on June 18.
  4. Make a donation — even $25 funds door-hangers for neighborhoods we haven't reached.
  5. Share this website — forward it to anyone in Evergreen who cares about the library.

Absolutely. You don't have to think of this as political to help. You can simply vote yes, encourage friends and neighbors to vote, or share the facts about what the library means to the community. You don't need to put a sign in your yard or call yourself a campaign supporter. Just show up and vote. That's enough.
